c.v: A medical malpractice claim in Michigan has rules no other injury claim has: a two-year deadline instead of three; a written Notice of Intent served on each provider at least 182 days before suit; a sworn Affidavit of Merit from a qualified expert filed with the complaint; strict rules on who that expert can be; and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages. A case that misses any one of them can be lost before its merits are heard. For a Waterford patient the first question is who the defendant is. Waterford Township has no hospital of its own. Many residents are treated at McLaren Oakland or Trinity Health Oakland, both a few minutes east in Pontiac and both Level II trauma centers on the State’s list, or for the most serious injuries at Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital in Royal Oak, the county’s Level I adult trauma center. Day-to-day care happens in the township’s medical offices, urgent care clinics, and outpatient centers in and around the township, where health-system-employed physicians practice alongside independent practices and separate physician groups. Each has its own legal entity, insurer, and notice address, and a federally funded clinic is sued under federal law on a different clock in a different court.

sections.heading: What malpractice is, and is not

c.v: A bad outcome is not malpractice. Malpractice is a bad outcome caused by a provider who failed to do what a reasonably competent provider in the same specialty would have done in the same circumstances (MCL 600.2912a). You must prove the standard of care, a breach, that the breach more likely than not caused the injury, and damages. Michigan requires proof that the patient would have had a better outcome; a lost chance of a better outcome is compensable only where that chance was greater than 50 percent (MCL 600.2912a(2)). A qualified physician’s written review of the records decides, before anything is filed, whether a case exists. Many do not, and we say so.

sections.heading: Waterford’s providers, and who answers for each

c.v: McLaren Oakland and Trinity Health Oakland.

The two hospitals in Pontiac that treat many Waterford patients, both listed as Level II trauma centers, and their employed physicians, nurses, and staff. Trinity Health Oakland was formerly St. Joseph Mercy Oakland, and health-system names and ownership change, so the correct legal entity for the Notice of Intent must be identified from current corporate filings and from the name the hospital used at the time of care, not from the sign or the letterhead. Claims against either hospital and its employed providers are filed in the Sixth Judicial Circuit Court (Oakland County Circuit Court) in Pontiac.
Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital.

The Level I adult trauma center in Royal Oak, where the most serious Waterford injuries, strokes, and cardiac emergencies may be transferred. A transfer case can involve two hospitals, two sets of physicians, and the transport between them, and the question is which delay or decision caused the harm. It is also in Oakland County, so the same circuit court hears it.
Emergency physicians and other contracted groups.

Many hospitals staff their emergency departments, anesthesia, and radiology through separate physician groups. The Notice of Intent must name the group as well as the hospital. Medical offices, urgent care, surgery centers, and imaging centers.

The primary-care and specialty practices, urgent care clinics, and outpatient surgery, endoscopy, and imaging centers that serve Waterford in and around the township. A delayed diagnosis in an office practice, a missed fracture or infection at urgent care, and a surgical complication at an outpatient center are frequent claims, and the employer of each provider who touched the chart must be identified, because a health-system-employed physician and an independent physician in the same building are different defendants with different insurers. Michigan rules apply.

Health centers that receive federal Health Center Program funding, including centers serving Pontiac and the surrounding townships, can have their providers deemed federal employees for malpractice purposes. A claim against one follows the Federal Tort Claims Act, not Michigan procedure: an administrative claim on Standard Form 95 to the Department of Health and Human Services within two years (28 USC 2401(b)), no Notice of Intent, and suit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, tried to a judge without a jury. Identifying a deemed clinic early is the difference between a timely claim and none.

Veterans treated at the John D. Dingell VA Medical Center in Detroit or a VA outpatient clinic have an FTCA claim on the same path, and may also qualify for disability compensation under 38 USC 1151 where the injury was caused by VA carelessness, negligence, or error, or by an event that was not reasonably foreseeable; see our VA benefit claims page.

Waterford’s emergency medical services are provided by the Waterford Regional Fire Department. Claims against EMS personnel, and against the agency that employs them, public or private, including a private ambulance company handling a transfer between hospitals, are limited by the Emergency Medical Services Act to gross negligence or willful misconduct (MCL 333.20965(1)).

faqs.question: How long do I have to sue a doctor or hospital after care in Waterford or Pontiac?

answer.v: Two years from the malpractice, with a six-month discovery rule capped at six years. Because the Notice of Intent must be served 182 days before suit and the expert review comes first, call well inside the first year.

faqs.question: Is the Notice of Intent “six months” or 182 days?

answer.v: 182 days, which is not the same as six calendar months. A notice served on the last day of a six-month count can be late. Count the days.

faqs.question: I was sent home from urgent care and it turned out to be serious. Is that malpractice?

answer.v: It can be, if a reasonably careful provider would have recognized the warning signs or ordered the test, and the delay changed the outcome. The urgent care operator, not the hospital system whose name may be on the building, is often the employer, so the right defendant has to be identified first.

faqs.question: I was transferred from a Pontiac hospital to Royal Oak. Which hospital is responsible?

answer.v: It depends on where the decision or delay that caused the harm happened: the first hospital’s diagnosis and decision to transfer, the transport, or the care after arrival. Each provider is a separate defendant with its own Notice of Intent.

faqs.question: I’m a veteran and was treated at the VA. Is that different?

answer.v: Yes. A claim against VA care follows the Federal Tort Claims Act: an administrative claim within two years, no Notice of Intent, and suit in federal court without a jury. A veteran may also qualify for disability compensation for an injury caused by VA error or an unforeseeable event.

faqs.question: My care was at a community health center. Is that different?

answer.v: It may be. If the center is federally funded and its providers are deemed federal employees, the claim is against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act. We check the center’s status at the first call.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on what I can recover?

answer.v: On pain-and-suffering damages only: $596,400 in the standard case and $1,065,000 for the catastrophic permanent injuries the statute lists, in 2026, adjusted each year. Medical bills, lost earnings, and future care are not capped.

faqs.question: My child was injured at birth. How long do we have?

answer.v: A child injured before age eight has until the tenth birthday to file. The parents’ own claims are subject to the ordinary two-year period, so the family should not wait.
